newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Ozone hole in check but recovery seen years away.
newsitem.headline: Ozone hole in check but recovery seen years away.

text.p: There is promising evidence the hole in the ozone layer is getting no worse, but the damage already done may not start to heal for more than a decade, scientists at a conference said this week.

Experts gathered in Ushuaia, the southernmost city in the world, said the gap that opens every year over the Antarctic is no bigger than usual. The ozone layer shields Earth from the sun's harmful ultraviolet rays.

But trafficking in chemicals that eat away at the layer, together with delays in banning them, could delay the recovery process and expose people for years to come to increased levels of cancer-causing UB-V radiation.

"Between now and 2005-2010 we can expect exactly the same conditions of (ozone-depleting) chlorine in the stratosphere, and the same amount of ozone destruction," said Rumen Bojkov, special adviser to the World Meteorological Organisation.

"Besides, in any given year we could have a stronger impact, depending on meteorological conditions, because for example we know that lower temperatures may cause even greater ozone depletion," the Hungarian-born physicist, who also chairs the International Ozone Commission, told Reuters.

Bojkov and other specialists were participating in a three-day workshop ending on Friday on health and radiation in Ushuaia, one of the few cities exposed to the hole when it tips over from Antarctica to the Southern Cone between September and mid-October -- this year for a record six days.

The ozone layer began peeling away in the 1970s due to the effects of man-made chemicals, mainly chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), used in refrigerators and other cooling systems. Global ozone depletion now stands at around six percent.

But in the past four years the hole -- a special condition that forms over Antarctica because of the unique weather system of the polar vortex, where depletion exceeds 60 percent -- has mostly stabilised.
The hole is open for four and a half months until mid-December and measures 8.5 million square miles (22 million square km) at its peak. No significant change is likely this year, Bojkov said.

That is partly thanks to revisions of the Montreal Protocol, a swift phase-out plan for the offending chemicals crafted in 1987 under which developed countries last year stopped production and imports of CFCs.

"The protocol has been very successful in slowing down the buildup of major ozone-depleting substances," James Shevlin, assistant director of ozone protection at the Australian Environmental Protection Agency, said.
Because CFCs take up to eight years to reach the stratsophere, however, there is a big lag effect and no improvements may be seen until 2010, Shevlin said.

In the best-case scenario, the layer will have totally recovered by the middle of the next century. "That is provided all countries observe the protocol and stop illegal traffic in CFCs," said Ruben Piacentini, director of the Astronomical Observatory of Rosario, Argentina. "Otherwise we don't know what the delays could be."

India and China may be dragging their feet in switching out of CFCs, according to some experts, while Russia has formally delayed phase-out plans by five years. Meanwhile smuggling of banned chemicals exists because it is cheaper to keep old air conditioning sets working on CFCs.
"In the United States CFCs are the second biggest illegal item brought in after cocaine in terms of value," a foreign protocol negotiator, who asked not to be named, told Reuters.
